title: 'Prisons are inherently dangerous places,' attorney general contends in defence against Van Camp family's lawsuit
subtitle: In a statement of defence filed on May 11, the attorney general said "Prisons are inherently dangerous places."
article: Bit by bit, Lauren Laithwaite has been finding out what happened before her son, Chris Van Camp, died in custody at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary last June.

A year after her son's death, RCMP finally told her the cause of his death at the age of 37, "And even though I found out really awful things, that's better than not knowing," she said, fighting back tears.

Van Camp was found unresponsive in his cell the morning on June 7, 2017, less than 24 hours after he was transferred to the maximum security unit at the Prince Albert. His cellmate, Tyler Vandewater, is charged with second-degree murder in connection with his death.

Laithwaite named federal Attorney General Jody Wilson-Raybould and the Correctional Service of Canada in a lawsuit alleging prison staff knowingly placed an ill Van Camp in "the unsupervised proximity of an extremely violent inmate." The allegations in the suit have not been tested in court.
In a statement of defence filed on May 11, the attorney general said Van Camp's death was not foreseeable and that "Prisons are inherently dangerous places."

"In answer to the plaintiffs' claim as a whole, Van Camp led a high risk lifestyle that put him into contact with other criminals, including criminal gangs. The assault, on or about June 7, 2017, on his first day back at Saskatchewan Penitentiary Maximum Unit was a direct result of his high risk lifestyle. While previously incarcerated, Van Camp had been found in possession of stabbing weapons and had participated in drug related incidents," the statement added.
Laithwaite's lawyer, Tavengwa Runoywa, calls the attorney general's statement of defence a step too far.

"What I found unacceptable was the idea they'd allude to this notion that Chris was a bad guy, ended up in a bad place with other bad guys and he got murdered and that's life. Obviously, that's not how it's framed verbatim, but that is certainly the significance of what's in that statement."

Runoywa said the argument ignores the fact that the attorney general and corrections staff have a duty to ensure inmates are as safe as humanly possible, that they have access to proper health care facilities and that correctional institutions provide the necessities of life.
He's asking the attorney general's counsel to retract this part of the defence.
The StarPhoenix contacted the Department of Justice's Saskatoon office but no response was received before press time.

Laithwaite and Runoywa contend that Van Camp should never have been returned to custody at Saskatchewan Penitentiary or its maximum security unit after he overdosed, under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act, passed last May.
Under the act, no one who calls 911 because they or someone else is overdosing will be charged with violating release conditions if the evidence was found as a result of seeking help.
"If you put aside the idea of 'things happen in prison,' the most important thing is that he was never supposed to be in prison in the first place," Runowya said.
Laithwaite said she called Van Camp's parole officer after he overdosed on May 24, 2017, a month after he was granted statutory release with the condition he abstain from drug and alcohol use.
She said this is what kills her: That she followed every rule.
Her son only had to report to his parole officer twice a month after the first month had passed, she said, adding that her son had a treatment centre to go to in hospital.

"And he assured me there'd be no more re-arrest," Laithwaite said. "And then he told me it was out of his hands, because his supervisor - he didn't say it was his supervisor at the time - he just said it was out of his hands."
Van Camp was comatose for days after the overdose, then was rearrested and taken to Bowden Institution in Alberta before he was moved to the Saskatchewan Penitentiary.
Laithwaite said she recently obtained some of her son's documents from the CSC, including the transfer and arrest warrant.

The attorney general's position, in its statement of defence, is that a maximum security institution can't be expected to supervise all inmates at all times. It also states Van Camp and Vandewater had previously been cellmates without problems earlier that year and when Van Camp returned to custody, he didn't raise concerns about his cellmate.
The murder charge against Vandewater, as well as aggravated assault charges against him, are scheduled for a pre-trial hearing Oct. 19 at Prince Albert's Court of Queen's Bench.
A coroner's inquest into Van Camp's death is also expected to take place.
Laithwaite has been honouring her son's memory by starting a group to help others, CV Angels. Volunteers distribute food at a Calgary rehab and drop-in centre.
"He was very loving and kind - I miss him dearly," she said.
